speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: RENTAL HOUSING PROJECT-NEW PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPRECIATION, AMORTIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during my remarks in this house on February 7 I stated that the government would shortly take steps to increase the supply of privately-ow'ned rental housing. At that time, I outlined three proposed incentives: (1) allowance of double depreciation for new rental housing units; (2) a longer period of amortization under the National Housing Act for loans on approved types of rental housing; and (3) extension of priorities for materials to assist in the construction of approved rental housing.
As I mentioned in February, our supply of new rental housing is proportionately too low and there is a great need in the country today for this type of dwelling. Perhaps the principal reason for the reluctance of private owners to enter this field is their belief that present capitalized costs may be high in relation to stabilized rents.
To stimulate an additional supply of rental housing, I now table order in council P.C. 1095 which provides for depreciation at double the rates normally allowed in respect to rental housing projects and equipment installed therein, built or acquired in a fixed period.
As hon. members know, the owner of a rental property, on filing income tax returns, is allowed as a deduction from the property value depreciation for buildings at standard rates which vary from two or five per cent, depending on the type of structure. In the case of equipment, these standard rates vary from five to ten per cent. The order in council I have just tabled has the effect of doubling these rates for a period of ten years when applied to projects consisting of four or more family dwelling units which meet the requirements set out in the order. This incentive will apply only to the types of rental housing approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Basic qualifications include rentals under $70 a month, based on a standard four-room unit; veterans' preference for occupancy of completed units; and an average of at least 1-75 bedrooms per unit.

Rental Housing Project
The order provides that:
Any project, wholly constructed between March 31, 1947, and December 31, 1949, will be allowed double depreciation on the full cost of construction.
Any project under construction on March 31, 1947, will be allowed double depreciation on costs incurred after that date.
Any project not completed by December 31, 1949, will be allowed double depreciation only on costs incurred prior to that date.
While I do not wish to discuss the order in detail at this time, I would point out to hon. members that provision is made for an extra principal payment by the owner of a rental property where the project is financed by mortgage. The extra principal payment required amounts to one-third of the allowable extra depreciation.
Hon. members may also be wondering why the effective date has been advanced to March 31. Under the order, the owner of a project at present under way who proposes to apply for double depreciation must obtain from a qualified architect or engineer a certificate of costs of the project at that date. The advanced date will allow him time to do so.
To determine whether or not a rental housing project qualifies for double depreciation under the provisions of this order, a builder will be required to complete and file an application with a regional or branch office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Full information may also be obtained from these offices, which are located in principal cities throughout the country. If a project is found to qualify, the corporation will issue a certificate of entitlement.
Increased amortization. Tlje second point I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks was an extended period of amortization. We will introduce shortly legislation under the National Housing Act to increase to thirty years the period of amortization for this type of rental housing.
Priorities. As a third stimulation, priorities for building materials will be granted for rental housing projects which meet the same requirements as those set out in the order respecting double depreciation. While I am on the subject, I wish to take this opportunity to reaffirm the government's position with respect to priorities. During the past few weeks, it has come to my attention that certain groups are apparently anticipating a relaxation of the priorities policy. I wish to state emphatically that the government does not now propose to revise the present system,
which is based on a veterans' preference and some control over the end sales price or rent to be charged for housing units.
So that there can be no misunderstanding or confusion, I list again the housing categories entitled to priorities on materials:
1.	The house of any individual veteran of world war II where the house is fifty per cent completed, which generally means roofed and closed in.
2.	All government and government-sponsored housing carrying the veterans' preference, such as that built under the integrated housing plan, Veterans Land Act, and emergency shelter order and by Wartime Housing Limited and Housing Enterprises of Canada, Limited.
3.	Housing in remote areas built by basic industries such as lumbering, logging, mining and fishing companies, for which the rentals or sale prices of the units are approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and where an undertaking is given by the company that fifty per cent of the units will be occupied by veterans of world war II.
4.	Rental housing projects, as I already stated, which meet the same requirements as those set out in the order I have tabled today respecting double depreciation.

speechtext:
In the absence of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) may I be permitted to give a few words of explanation? The proposed amendments refer to sections 15 and 32 of Bill No. 14 as passed in this house last February. Section 15 of the bill amended section 46 of the Militia Act. It referred to certain restrictions on the wearing of uniforms. The proposed amendment does substantially the same thing but it is reworded to make it clearer and less ambiguous.
Section 32, which amended section 139 of the Militia Act, refers to the power given to the governor general in council to empower the minister to make certain regulations. When this section was studied by the senate the remark was made that the amendment as wordied implied that it was rather the exception than the rule for the governor general in council to make regulations. It was pointed out that the paramount authority in the act was for the governor general in council to make regulations, and any exception to that rule would be by the governor general in council empowering the minister to do so. Consequently the section was redrafted to make this implication clear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot agree with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence that the senate amendment makes clearer the amendment to section 46 as passed in this house. I suggest that the amendment now under consideration changes the meaning of the amendment adopted in this house; it does not merely change the words. The words of bill 14 amending old section 46 of the act read:
No unit-
By "unit" I understand is meant an organized body of troops.
No unit or man, other than a unit or man of the active force or a warrant officer shall at any time appear in uniform or armed or accoutred, except . . .
Militia Act

Then it gives certain exceptions. The amendment suggested by the other place reads:
No unit warrant officer or man other than a unit warrant officer or man of the active force shall at any time appear in uniform or armed or accoutred, except . . .
The essential difference is that the privilege which has always been granted to a warrant officer to appear in uniform on the streets, or to attend any function in uniform without having to go to his commanding officer and get his consent, is now removed by this amendment which has been suggested by the other place. I suggest that it is not of national importance but it is a prerogative and a privilege which has been enjoyed for many years by senior warrant officers who served in the old non-permanent militia, which is today known as the reserve army.
When our amendment to the old act was introduced it seemed to me that care was taken that that privilege should be continued. In this proposed amendment the warrant officer, who up to the present has had the same privileges so far as the wearing of uniform is concerned as the commissioned officer, is having these privileges taken away from him. I do not know what the procedure is, but I do suggest that this amendment, as it changes the meaning of our bill, should be referred back to the other place, or that a further discussion should be had, or some other means taken to rectify the matter. As I say, it is not a matter of vital national importance, but it is a privilege which has been cherished by those people in the reserve army, in the non-permanent militia, who have voluntarily given up their time. Sometimes these niceties of the services are highly appreciated, and it will be resented if they are taken away without just cause.
There are some other comments that I should like to make regarding this suggested amendment. It uses the words, "no unit warrant officer." Well, of course, all warrant officers are not on the strength of a unit, and it would seem to me this gives a warrant officer who is not on the strength of a unit the right to wear uniform at the same time as officers without having to apply to the commanding officer, but denies this privilege to the warrant officer who is serving with a unit. I do not believe the other place intended to make these alterations, and if it can be referred back perhaps the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) can adjust it with the movers of the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one observation. It will be so short that hon. members on the other side will be glad to hear it. There has been over the last few days a good deal of discussion with respect to this legislation. Perhaps some issues may have become clarified and others not. Perhaps some new issues have been brought in. I should like it made clear to the house and country that in this regard I speak on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party as a whole, and I repeat what was stated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) at the beginning of the debate. It is only proper and fitting that at this stage we should indicate again the position this party took, namely that we were prepared to allow the resolution to go through and would not on the resolution stage take our stand with respect to the principle of the bill to follow. Rather it was stated that we were prepared to allow the resolution to pass; and it was understood that while in committee of the whole we would seek from the government the information we needed respecting the stand we would take subsequently on the bill itself.
There were however a number of things which intervened, with the result that many

Emergency Powers
hon. members made speeches. We are now in the same position as that which we occupied at that time. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house, that we reserve now, as we did then, the right either to support or to oppose the bill on second reading, after the information we shall seek in committee stage has been given to us by the government. The whole debate, from our point of view, will of course be relegated to the motion for second reading of the bill. On that basis, and strictly without prejudice to our rights as a party to take such stand as we may think is proper and desirable or in the public interest, we are now prepared to allow the resolution to pass.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I wish to say a few words on this resolution. The time has come for this country to get rid of dictatorial powers which no longer have any justification. There is a limit to unwarranted emergency measures. The war has been over for almost two years. The government mobilized all our resources to crush dictatorship. But they are asking us now to surrender our prerogatives as representatives of the people to an irresponsible bureaucracy. This army of officials has taken the place of parliament much too long. All civil servants, clerks and employees look down patronizingly on those whose mandate they have usurped. The people are surfeited with this bureaucracy which has implanted in Canada a loathsome form of dictatorship. We owe nothing to all these boards, save inflation and the black market. In a country like ours, so rich in natural resources, there is no ground for imposing rations conducive to hoarding, simulation and fraud.
I have had many an opportunity, in my professional capacity, of representing persons amenable to a court which had been prosecuted by the wartime prices and trade board. Invariably, the seller only was summoned. The buyer, who had also broken the law, always got off scot-free. No action was brought against him. Such justice is not worthy of the name. I have heard some magistrates denounce, with reason, the procedure followed by those bureaucrats who, daily, break our laws, both federal and provincial.
For too many years, under cover of the 'national emergency arising from the war" the most flagrant infractions of our federal and provincial laws have been perpetrated under the guise of controls. The astonishing statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) bears me out. In the first place, he contended that even in peace time the dominion parliament may legislate in a field reserved to the provinces when it is necessary to do so in order to maintain peace, order and good government, etc. That is the pet phrase so dear to the hearts of those who have supported the extravagant expenditures made in war time. Were it only for that statement of the Minister of Justice I would have a thousand reasons to reject his resolution. I cannot have any faith in the man who unscrupulously builds up a bureaucracy upon the ruins of parliamentary prerogatives. I respect the views expressed by the Minister of Justice, but I cannot conceive how anyone can make such a statement of policy eighty years after confederation.
For years the dominion government has striven unceasingly to assimilate and centralize. Taking advantage of the word "war," it launched into the great adventure and never returned. This is proved by the fact that we are still squatting under the Moscow conference table. Denied a part in the conference of the Big Four, it is forced to while away its time cultivating socialism and consolidating an already flourishing bureaucracy. The same old reason will be used in justification of controls: "Inflation must be avoided." Come now, inflation is here despite all controls. Anyone buying property will have to pay four times the price of 1939 or 1940. Build your own home and it will cost you much more than a few years ago. Walk into your dealer's, your grocer's or any place of business, and you shall find that the price of commodities, of clothes for instance, has increased enormously. In the case of clothes and many other prime necessities, prices have gone up as high as 200 and 300 per cent. On top of this, consider the burdensome taxes that have to be paid especially by the small wage earner, and you shall have the sad picture of the pernicious results of controls and bureaucracy.
And now, with this resolution, the government would have parliament allow bureaucracy to carry on? For my part, I refuse any longer to surrender parliament's prerogatives to a bureaucracy that keeps exploiting the people under the cloak of ultra vires legislation brought in by a parliament which is giving up its mandate.
Under pretext of urgency, the government slash our statutes and constitution. Centralization and assimilation lead us directly to legislative union.
I represent a constituency which took up arms to fight the dictatorship of bureaucracy. More than a century has elapsed since this pathetic struggle. Canada has taken part in the two largest wars of history for the sake of the four freedoms as defined in the Atlan-
Emergency Powers

tic charter. In a helpless world, I seek in vain for even a shadow of these freedoms. What has become of all these loftiest ideologies which we have defended: Christianity, freedom, justice and right? In our own country, provincial rights granted by the constitution are infringed upon in the name of a so-called national emergency. Freedom, justice and right, for which our soldiers laid down their lives, have become idle words. Among those who lived through the struggle, how many are looking in vain for a shelter, while our building materials are being controlled or shipped outside the country? Such is, in all its ghastliness, the work of a bureaucracy unanswerable to the people. I shall fight this regime without let-up for it is a source of centralization and injustice on which the parliament elected by the people have no control whatever.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while not an advocate of repetition I deem it my duty to express my views on this resolution. First of all I am in complete agreement with the stand taken by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) on the first night of debate of this resolution. I think his exposition, argument and presentation were logical and strictly in accord with democratic socialism and given with a view to the requirements of the people of this country. I do not think there is any necessity at this time for me to attempt to repeat those arguments or the arguments that many other members have put forward in this debate.
I listened particularly with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and to his argument in opposition to this resolution. That is significant. I have listened, with a great deal of interest to the arguments, or, should I say, to the declamations of the members of the Progressive Conservative party. I think they are

In the first place it is for the benefit at this time under these circumstances of the great majority of the Canadian people, and in the second place the socialists are given to thinking logically about economic questions, and this resolution from our point of view is logical in a concrete way. I just want to say again that I think our good friends in the Progressive Conservative ranks ' are too much disturbed over the possible socialist contents of this resolution and the legislation that will follow.
I want us to look at this resolution for a very few moments without prejudice, and from a non-partisan point of view, because I think the country is looking at it on the whole with a non-partisan view.
First of all, controls were definitely necessary during the war and were supported by the great majority of the Canadian people. There is no question about that. Secondly,

Emergency Powers
controls worked during the war to the great advantage of our war effort and without doubt proved our ability successfully to overcome the common enemy. My third point is this, that as the result of our war experience and as the result of what is happening in other countries, and no one can deny this, the great majority of the Canadian people, realizing the value of these controls during the critical war period and now, are expressing their support for a continuation of controls particularly while commodities are in short supply. I think that is generally recognized, and no one can deny it. The evidence is found in the stand taken by organized labour, by the organized farmers, by large groups of consumers, throughout the country, by church organizations and by many women's organizations. So far as my riding is concerned I know that when I stand here and support this resolution I am expressing the will and the opinion and the desire of the great majority of the people I have the honour to represent.

To the Progressive Conservatives I would say this. If they have read carefully British, Australian and New Zealand papers and the papers of the United States in past years, they will have found repeated references to the successful operaton of controls in Canada, made by the press not only of the Liberal party, of the Labour party and of the Socialist party, but of the Conservative party in all these countries.
I want to quote something which the bureau of agricultural economics in Washington reported recently. It reports that one dollar today will buy only as much food as 72 cents would have bought a year ago when price control was in effect in the United States. The bureau reports that between January 1946 and January 1947 retail food prices in the United States have risen as follows-and these are things that are vitally important to the people of this country: meats, 67 per cent; dairy products, 37 per cent; bakery and cereal products, 30 per cent; canned fruit and vegetables, 32 per cent.
In addition the National Retail Lumber Dealers Association of the United States from its executive offices in that country issued a .statement to the effect that in their opinion
home-building costs have increased 50 per cent in two years, and the United States section of Proctor and Gamble Company announce that tallow, a very important ingredient in soap, has climbed from 20 to 274 cents per pound recently, and that is going to be reflected in the cost of soap to consumers. It would be possible to go on for hours giving illustrations of the value of controls in this country as against the situation that has existed in the United States since the forgoing there of price control. '
I have heard it stated on many occasions and several times in this debate that controls will restrict production. I do not think that argument has any validity or is rooted in fact. One has only to examine the production figures of this country for the last two years, the balance sheets of all large industrial firms, or to read carefully the addresses made to the shareholders by the presidents of all the banks of Canada at their annual meetings, to realize that on the whole production never reached a greater height in Canadian history. I want to give one illustration of the absurd statements made at times by people occupying responsible executive positions in the industrial field. I have not one handy from a Canadian source, but I have one from an American source, and it is a gem, what you would call a beauty. I quote from an Associated Press dispatch from Philadelphia of a few days ago:
J. Howard Pew, President of the Sun Oil Company, said today that until government wartime controls are ended "industry cannot function efficiently and effectively to serve the nation."
One can almost hear the voice of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming).
He told stockholders in an annual report that Sun established new records in 1946 for crude oil production, refinery operation and marketing.
How can you place those two statements together?
That concludes my argument so far as this resolution is concerned. I support the principle of controls because experience has proved that oontrols are to the benefit of the great majority of the Canadian people and I have no fear of controls provided they are exercised as a result of action by this parliament.

the reason that the country is in a state of short supply. I am not going to argue that point, but I would say that if the country is in a state of short supply there must have been a reason for it, and I contend that government policy during the time that we have granted to them the power to exercise control under the emergency powers act has been largely the reason that goods are in short supply.
The hon. member mentioned that production has increased, but it is a well known fact that the government of the day have been so-I was going to use the term hell-bent, but that might not be appropriate for me-so desirous and covetous of foreign markets that they have permitted much of our production to go out of the country and thus by control have controlled to the minimum point the consumption of Canadian goods in Canada.
Again we have our price control. I voted in the past for giving to the government emergency powers to combat inflation, and I am not going to say they have not done a fair job under existing conditions in combating serious inflation. But there is another thing. When goods are in short supply, even by reason of exports, then prices are bound to rise. I was not going to speak along that line, and perhaps those few remarks will serve more or less as an introduction.
What I am concerned about is the principle involved in this measure, which as I see it is fundamentally the principle of controls placed in the hands of government rather than, where it belongs, in the hands of parliament or the people.
The member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) yesterday spent some considerable time in emphasizing the necessity for governments to have power. He expressed no fear that the present Prime Minister would deliberately give away the powers of parliament to somebody else. Of course that statement was carefully worded. I personally do not express any fear that the present Prime Minister would deliberately and knowingly do any such thing. That is not what we are in danger of. The thing that we are in danger of is that power ,s to be taken from us by stealth; that is the principle that is involved, and one has to make a decision between governmental power and the power of our parliamentary institutions.
He expressed no fear that the Minister of Agriculture or even the leader of the official opposition would deliberately give away those powers, because, he went on to say, the people of Canada have the right and power to punish those who may be guilty of such abuse by discharging them. Some objection has been taken to this bill on the ground that it includes about fifty-seven orders in council relating to controls. For this I think the minister and the government deserve congratulations for trying to expedite matters in this house. At the beginning of this session I advocated a change in the rules of the house in order to shorten the debates. Up to the present time may I say that we have taken about two months to do what we could have done in about two or three weeks at most. Usually, after scores of speeches and amendments have been presented by opposition groups, the measures of the government are adopted
exactly as they were moved. I again ask that we in this house do business in a businesslike manner. Personally I will take about ten minutes to express my views in this matter relating to controls.
May I say first that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) objected to the procedure- followed in this connection more than he objected to the substance of the bill itself. I repeat that the minister is to be congratulated upon bringing in this bill in the form in which he has brought it in. On this subject of controls, the government is taking, as usual, a moderate course. On the one hand, some of the Tories want to abolish all the controls immediately and suddenly, although, as they did on some other bills this session, they may finally vote for the bill. On the other hand, the C.C.F. want more controls than we already have. Following this is the opinion of the law officer of the Department of Justice which gives quite a body of jurisprudence and discusses a few cases such as the Temperance Act case, the Fort Frances pulp and paper case, and the Manitoba Free Press case in relation to the Natural Products Marketing Act of 1934 and the act for the sale and export of agricultural products of 1947. The deputy minister said:

The Minister of Justice then spoke as follows:

Yesterday the hon. member for Lake Centre put forward the view, not dogmatically but for the consideration of the government, that the doctrine of emergency no longer was valid as a basis for dominion jurisdiction.
It was not the minister who said that, it was the hon. member for Lake Centre. I continue with the quotation:

It will be easily seen therefore that there is no occasion or reason to think or

fear that this jurisprudence quoted in the legal opinion just referred to is to be implemented or translated into any definite or positive act or step or legislation whatsoever. The present measure relating to controls is not based on that legal point of view at all. Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, the resolution before this house is in effect to continue for a limited period certain orders and regulations passed by the governor in council under the War Measures Act. Further, the resolution is to authorize the governor in council to hire and to pay out of public funds an unfixed, undetermined amount to the numerous officers, clerks and employees of the wartime prices and trade board and the crown companies who will administer, execute and decide the limitation of freedom of the Canadian people for a limited period under these orders and regulations.
The resolution, as I understand it, assumes that a state of emergency still exists, and the debate has brought a statement of the law officers of the Department of Justice into

Emergency Powers
Hansard, that even if a state of national emergency did not exist de facto, it would still be lawful and constitutional under the "peace, order and good government" proviso of section 91 of the British North America Act to apply in peace time the orders and regulations which were passed under the War Measures Act and which, it is alleged, violate some of the provisions of section 92 of the British North America Act.
It could be stated here as an aside that if the officers of the Department of Justice who wrote that opinion had been expressly mandated to prepare an opinion which would furnish Messrs. Macdonald, Drew and Duples-sis precious ammunition in their fight for the respect of provincial autonomy, they could not have dona better. True, after the speeches made by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and the hon. member for Montmagnv-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), whose opinion I fully share, on the constitutional issue at present involved, and after the carefully timed question put by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret), the government has taken pains to restate, I would say, its constitutional views. But- and this is a big "but"-I have not heard or read yet that the advisers to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) had changed their own legal opinion on the same subject. Whether the right hon. minister will be able to convince his advisers or whether the advisers will reconvince the minister, I do not know. Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, the constitutional issue, although a most serious one, is not the only issue involved in this resolution.
In preceding debates and in the course of this debate, another highly controversial assertion has been brought into play. It has been stated that a national emergency in Britain creates a national emergency in Canada because, Britain being our best customer, if she does not remain so we shall ourselves immediately suffer dire economic consequences. The fact remains that our best customer is at the moment also our heaviest and least immediately-solvent debtor, despite the fact that this country has literally pumped into the economic heart of Britain, both during and since the war, billions of dollars in loans, goods and credits. Certainly Canada can never be accused of having been miserly in its help, even if Canada decided to discontinue that benevolence tomorrow, and set herself to do business with customers who are able to pay their bills immediately.
No one has greater admiration and sympathy than 1 have for the courageous British people in their present straits, and no one
wishes them a speedier recovery. Yet as a Canadian I cannot fail to take notice of the conditions prevailing in my own country, of the various shortages which handicap our own economic recovery and which create unrest and discontent among all classes, particularly the labouring and white-collar classes who, already deeply affected by small wages, cannot procure those few items of necessity or comfort to which as humans they are entitled.
As was so ably stated by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) last evening, you will never be able to convince the fishing community of Quebec's north shore that it must do without powdered milk. You cannot convince the Canadian farmer, who cannot procure a much-needed truck that he must do without it; similarly you cannot convince the veteran who cannot procure decent lodgings; the father of a family who has saved for years to build a small house of his own but cannot do so for lack of building materials; the rural dweller who wishes to have electricity installed, but cannot obtain wire and fixtures because they are nonexistent, except on the black market; the mother of a large family who cannot procure the butter she needs when she needs it because of our commitments to Britain and the necessity of keeping solvent our best customer. In all cases, to the man who is not acquainted with the intricacies of international finance and markets, the answer will be: "Well, ordained charity begins at home," and I know of no one who is prepared to challenge the truth of this old saying and wisdom. That we should export our own production surpluses, I agree, and say, "yes"; that we should export that portion of our production which is evidently needed here, I disagree and say "no". After all, there is a limit beyond which a nation of twelve million people, which bled itself in its magnificent war effort, cannot be asked to go even if it is to help its good customers. If controls are to be maintained for a further period, the boys at the controls should be instructed to control in such a way as to give to the Canadian people who pay their wages, those necessities, utilities and goods which are sorely needed, before controlling for purposes of exportation and favourable trade balances. Highly trained economists, and exponents of internationalism may believe that exportations come first, but the average Canadian thinks that, because he produces, pays the bills and the taxes, he comes first; and in that attitude I believe he is absolutely correct and honest.
The present resolution involves a still greater principle than constitutional integrity,

the opportunity of maintaining exports and helping our friends and erstwhile allies; it involves that principle which further consecrates a planned and controlled economy rather than a return to the old competitive system. One of these days, and maybe very soon, we shall have to make a definite choice. We cannot forever pay lip service to the cause of freedom of enterprise, the while fostering and abetting state control, state power, by looking to the government or to the bureaucrats to provide a way out of our economic difficulties.
Various opinions have from time to time been expressed in this house on this allimportant issue, opinions which vary all the way from out-and-out socialism to mitigated socialism, to mitigated capitalism and to rock-ribbed individualism.
To the believers in continued state control, I should like to read this extract from Time magazine of February 17, which is speaking about the communist Eisler, who is now in the hands of American justice:
But beyond Eisler there are a host of other men-fellow travellers, confused liberals, "totalitarian liberals," left-wing new dealers-who owe muddled allegiance to the idea that government should be omnipotently responsible for the lives of its citizens even to the point of benevolent despotism. They fail to understand that despotism, which has a way of beginning with benevolence, usually ends by being merely despotic. Few of them even understood the incompatibility of their views with democracy, or that it is just such views which makes them so sympathetic to Soviet Russia.
I should also like to read this extract from Friedrich A. Hayek's great book, "The Road to Serfdom":
In order to achieve their ends, the planners must create power-power over men wielded by other men . . . Their success will depend on the extent to which they achieve such power. Democracy is on obstacle to .this suppression of freedom which the centralized direction of economic activity requires. Hence arises the clash between planning and democracy.
And further:
To decentralize power is to reduce the absolute amount of power, and the competitive system is the only system designed to minimize the power exercised by man over man. Who can seriously doubt that the power which a millionaire, who may be my employer, has over me is very much less than that which the smallest bureaucrat possesses who wields the coercive power of the state and on whose discretion it depends how- I am allow-ed to live and work.
And still further:
Our generation has forgotten that the system of private property is the most important guarantee of freedom. It is only because the control of the means of production is divided among many people acting independently that w-e as

individuals can decide what to do with ourselves. When all the means of production are vested in a single hand, whether it be nominally that of "society" as a whole or that of a dictator, whoever exercises this control has complete power over us. In the hands of private individuals, what is called economic power can be an instrument of coercion, but it is never control over the w-hole life of a person. But when economic power is centralized as an instrument of political power it creates a degree of dependence scarcely distinguishable from slavery.
It can be argued, and quite properly, that the present resolution does not go that far and that it is a move to decontrol slowly; yet it is maintenance of controls in the most potent and dangerous of forms, namely, statutes. On this continuation of controls, I should like to quote two opinions. One is by the Canadian chamber of commerce passed at Winnipeg, and reads as follows:
The highest standard of living in the world has been developed on this continent under the system of private competitive enterprise. The Canadian chamber of commerce records its unswerving support for that system and its vigorous opposition to anything which would weaken or destroy the rights and freedom of the individual citizen.
Freedom of choice and freedom of action, within the limits of the public welfare are regarded as inalienable rights of the individual. The chamber holds that Canada can be great and prosperous only if all individuals have the incentive of adequate reward for energy-, initiative and enterprise and the right to enjoy the products of their thrift and foresight. Freedom is indivisible. The individual cannot be deprived of his economic freedom and retain his political freedom.
The rights of free citizens to sell the products of their labours cannot be surrendered to the state without a loss of personal liberties, such as few citizens would be willing to accept
The other quotation is from a statement made by Robert P. Jellett, chairman of the board of the Royal Trust Company, on February 11, 1947, and reads as follows:
There is need for much careful thought by all citizens as to the part that the state may properly exercise in the total of the country's activity. The attempt to regulate prices and wages has brought about a remarkable extension of the state's control. I have not believed, however, that any combination of brains at the disposal of governments can ever equal the almost automatic effects of the ordinary law of supply and demand in the efficient adjustment of prices and wages. There is a limit to the number of experts w-ho may be engaged to watch conditions, costs, and prices, and to endeavour to exercise control of them to the best interests of the economy of the country. But there is almost no limit to the number of people w-ho through their multitudinous purchases and sales bring about the changes in prices needed to balance supply and demand. A point to bear in mind is that these multitudes, in contrast to those employed in government bureaux and boards, render this essential service without cost to the taxpayer.

Emergency Powers
What is of still greater importance, only the prices established in this natural way can be regarded as genuine. The price levels established by bureaucratic manipulation are generally deceptive. For a low price can often be maintained only by the payment of subsidies or by the lowering of the quality of the goods- both of which must ultimately reduce the purchaser s income in other ways. Moreover, the artificial control of prices has led to many most undesirable complications, such as the encouragement of black marketing and the decline in the production of needed goods because the fixed prices do not make their manufacture profitable. It is well to face the fundamental economic fact that only free prices can tell the truth.
Return to Fundamentals
There are signs that people and government alike may be returning to the realization of the fundamental economic truth that whatever regulations may be found desirable in the public interest, the most natural and the most fruitful role of government comes from what it may be able to do to reduce all that restricts and'discourages, and to assist all that may release the )nimcasuruble potentialities that lie in free individual effort and responsibility.
Sir Ernest Benn has gone farther still: he has stated that a free trading competitive economy will not only prevent depressions, but also prevent wars. He spoke thus:
I am one of those who believe that but for the Ottawa agreements and our protective tariff at home, designed to save us from the supposed disadvantages of competition, Hitler would never have been heard of. I hold it to be a myth that wars of the past have been conducted for trade reasons or that economic competition has had anything whatever to do with them. At all events so far as we are concerned it is undoubtedly true that so long as we are prepared to buy and sell in the open market in competition with one and all, we offer no economic incentive to the most persistent of war-mongers.
It is then a matter for every hon. member to decide for himself, depending on the school of economics to which he belongs. As for me, I choose to align myself with the editors of Time, Freidrich Hayek, the Canadian chamber of commerce, Mr. R. P. Jellett, Sir Ernest Benn and countless Canadians who feel that full scope be given to the individual's initia-ti\ e. If this initiative runs amok, this house can legislate to curb it and punish it if needs be; but let this initiative, within law and reason, be given full speed ahead to hasten our economic recovery.
The resolution as it stands before us, Mr. Speaker, is too general in its terms. If a specific control were shown to be temporarily essential, by a specific measure, I would vote for it, except rentals, which should revert to provincial legislatures. If I can be shown that there is not enough butter, or cheese, or milk produced in this country to satisfy this country's needs, I will gladly vote to ration it; if it can be demonstrated that lumber is
not being produced in sufficient quantities to fill our construction needs, again I shall favour its control. But as regards lumber, I must say that producers feel that control is not further necessary, and I wish to put on Hansard copy of a letter written by the Canadian International Paper Company to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), permission for quotation having been obtained from the Canadian International Paper Company. The letter is dated February 17, 1947, and reads as follows:
Hon. Brooke Claxton, K.C.,
Minister of National Defence,
M.P. for St. Lawrence-St. George,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
We are of the opinion, along with other Canadian lumbermen, that the time has arrived when price control should be abolished and the lumber industry allowed to function in its own way.
Our cost of production has increased-in fact, above our present ceiling price, owing to increases of wages, food, supplies, especially labour, which makes up about 60 per cent of our total cost. This increase has forced us to look to foreign markets in order to balance the low prices of Canadian ceilings. This situation, if not checked, will jeopardize Canadian position in the world markets.
If decontrol is put into effect promptly, graded lumber will flow more freely under free distribution. Also the results of decontrol have been demonstrated by conditions in the United States where prices increased for a short period but settled down to a lower level; in some cases below the old OPA prices.
If decontrol is to be put into effect, the most opportune time would be at once, before the new production comes onto the market in early spring and summer.
We believe that you would be benefiting the country as a whole and the lumber industry in general by urging your cabinet members at Ottawa to have lumber controls removed.
Yours truly,
Canadian International Paper Company (Signed) G. G. Goodal],
Lumber Sales Manager.
I should also like to quote a paragraph from a letter of the Western Retail Lumberman's Association, dated February 27, 1947, which reads as follows:
Retail lumber dealers ask that price control on lumber be removed, firmly convinced that this course alone will restore order in the business and make possible increased volume of construction work.
For all the reasons I have given above, and because the resolution is too general in its terms and perpetuates government by order in council and administration of officers, clerks and employees not responsible to this house or to the people, I shall vote against it, and in so doing I believe I shall be in distinguished company.
Emergency Powers

I have chosen Vancouver and Seattle; Winnipeg and Minneapolis; Toronto and Detroit and Cleveland; Ottawa and Syracuse; Montreal and Boston. This survey was made between January 6 and 17. I find that, while milk sold in Canadian cities at from twelve to sixteen cents, it sold for from twenty-two to twenty-six cents in the United States. Perhaps I should explain that in making this comparison the fact that the Canadian imperial quart is larger than the United States quart was taken into account. The former O.P.A. ceiling price in the United States on milk was twenty to twenty-four cents. Creamery butter in Canadian cities sold at from forty-one to forty-six cents, and in the United States at from seventy-five to ninety-one cents, the former O.P.A. price being fifty-five to sixty-three cents. Cheese, which sold in

Canada at thirty-one to forty-two cents, sold a United States cities at from forty-six to sixty-nine cents, and the O.P.A. price had been forty-three to sixty-one cents.
All down the list of foodstuffs we find these marked differences in flour, corn syrup, soap- all the items used in Canadian homes. The effect of the removal of price ceilings in the United States has been that the citizens get less for their dollar. I am much happier to be in Canada than I would be if I were in the United States. True, certain wages and prices would appear more favourable on the surface, but I believe, on balance, conditions in Canada are a good deal better.
When the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) rises in the House of Commons he always makes an interesting speech. The hon. member might have gone on to develop an argument which was started some time ago regarding the town and country planning bill in the United Kingdom. Over there they have a set of conditions under which the ownership of the great resources of the country is vested in the hands of a small number of people. I saw that in an article which appeared in the Toronto Star Weekly of March 15, regarding this vicious socialist legislation, as it would be described by the Progressive Conservative party, Matthew Halton. C.B.C. correspondent, said this:
The measure is obviously then revolutionary. It is no wonder that one socialist journal calls it the end of the bastille'', while another headlines its story, ''Death to Debrett's " The land has always been the bastille of privilege in Britain, and a fortress hitherto inviolable [DOT] .	*. A handful of men owned the land of
Britain, and still do; but their tenure, or at least their control, is now to end. Of the 45,000,000 people in the United Kingdom, less than 2.900,000 own a single square foot of land. Of the 9.000.000 people in London less than 40.000 own a piece of land.
In the United Kingdom there are 90.000 square miles of land. Half of it is owned by 340 men. Lord Derby owns one-third of Lancashire The Duke of Norfolk owns 50,000 acres, the Earl of Breadalbane 300,000 acres, the Duke of Devonshire 180,000 acres, the Duke of Portland 183,000 acres, and so on. Just before the war the Marquis of Bute sold half the city of Cardiff for $150,000,000-and still owned 117.000 acres.
The ancient families own the land by ancient right or reward or accident or plunder. Typical example: Five hundred years ago at the battle of Tewkesbury, which ended the Wars of the Roses. Lord Stanley deserted Richard III at the crisis of the battle and went over to Henry 83160-110
\II and the Lancastrians. King Henry rewarded the traitor with the earldom of Derby and with the lands of the Lancastrians who had fought against him. Today, Lord Derby owns whole towns that have grown up on the lands so acquired, some $9,000.000- quite a substantial profit at that figure.
If I were living in Great Britain I would be advocating a land policy different from that advocated in Canada by the C.C.F. The fact is that in Canada the land belongs to the farmers, but they are not exploiting the consumers. It is a well-established fact that the Canadian farmers, in war time and in peace time, have worked unreasonably long hours and have produced enormous quantities of foods for local and foreign consumption. They have supplied these foodstuffs at less than the cost of production.
Therefore there is no reason under the sun why any political party in Canada should advocate a land policy such as that being advocated by the labour government in Great Britain, where we find a small handful of people owning vast estates and exploiting the people who work on that property.

For instance, the Woods Manufacturing Company is reported in today's paper as having made a net profit of $197,315 in 1945, and $302,610 in 1946. I submit that their position does not deserve very much sympathy.
Then, International Nickel, one of our very poor relations, showed a net profit in 1945 of $25,010,938, and in 1946 one of $29,681,352. Having said that much on the comments made by the members of the Progressive Conservative party, I want now to support the view expressed by the leader of this group and by my colleagues, that we are not satisfied with the government's disorderly retreat from the whole price control field. Calling the Minister of Justice a socialist is, I think, unfair. I believe that members in all parts of the house had a great admiration for the Minister of Justice in his capacity as Minister of Finance during the war. There was a good deal of sniping at many of the dictatorial powers that he took, -but I shall be surprised if any evidence is ever presented to show that the Minister of Justice in his position as Minister of Finance improved in any particular the financial position of himself or any of his friends, and I submit that that is an important test to apply to an organization which had such sweeping power and control over the lives of so many people. There can be no argument about it, that if Canada was to make her greatest contribution in prosecuting the war to a successful conclusion some authority had to decide the quantities of materials that should be allotted for domestic consumption and what quantities should be devoted to the manufacturing of armaments and supplying the necessities of our allies. During the war from 1914 to 1918 we got through without any of these controls, but in that war we diverted only about ten per cent of our national production to wTar purposes, while from 1939 to 1945 we diverted nearly fifty per cent and the interesting feature is that after we had diverted fifty per cent of our domestic consumption to war purposes, and after 750,000 of our youngest and finest went forth in the armed forces, our Canadian citizens at home enjoyed on the average, a higher standard of living than they had ever done before. I see that my hon. friend the member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) is about to interrupt me and tell me what the income tax did to him and how his way of life was cramped, and I am not denying that.

purposes. But controls were introduced, and the Canadian people, in response to appeals made by the government were prepared to get along without new cars, were content to drive their old ones, and put up with the rationing of gasoline.
It is unfortunate that some hon. members should have made such wild and reckless statements as to the extent of black markets in Canada. While there has been some black market business, I think that, on the whole, only a very small amount of business has been transacted on the black market. I did a good deal of travelling during the war and sometimes found myself arriving at a hotel without having made reservations in advance, but never once did I offer a bribe to any of the staff to get me a room. Sometimes I had to wait for some time and I did have to stay up all night on one occasion, but generally speaking I believe that the staff in hotels and stores and garages, in fact all our people, cooperated with the authorities in complying with the regulations.
I think it was the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Ashby) who suggested that all the deputy ministers should be called before the courts of justice and charged with treason. I believe that suggestion did a great disservice to public spirited citizens. The deputy ministers are not here to defend themselves, but each has a minister who must take responsibility for everything he did, and if any deputy minister has acted in an undemocratic way or has advocated things that are not in the public interest, the way to proceed against him is to get the minister on the carpet and make charges or bring the matter up on a question of privilege.
Again I suggest that we should determine for ourselves whether we would have had a more effective war effort without controls, whether it would have been better to allow the dollar ballots to decide what should be done.

The effect of the order has been the elimination of at least 100,000,000 truck miles per annum (this is an ultra conservative figure), with few instances where justifiable criticism based on actual hardship can be levelled at the board, either through lack of service or increased costs.

Mr. Speaker, when
the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) was speaking on Thursday he made reference to the housing problem which still exists in this country, and he said:
While much progress has been made in expanding our peace-time production, and while the flow of output is gathering increasing momentum, production in a number of important fields has not yet overtaken the high level of demand which in some cases, like that of housing, has been accumulating for years.
He was understating a pretty obvious fact. Later on, he said:
In some cases, the consequences are quite obvious. For example, I do not think there can be much question as to what would happen if the controls over rentals and evictions were removed in present circumstances. In the face of the continuing shortage of housing accommodation, it is clear enough that rents would rise sharply and that evictions would be counted in the tens of thousands.
The minister was interrupted by some of my Progressive Conservative friends over here who said "Oh, oh." The minister at once replied:
Absolutely true; and anyone who denies it is just living apart from the facts.
There have been suggestions from the Progressive Conservative section of the house that if all controls were abandoned, if free enterprise or private enterprise could have its: way, the housing problem would be solved next week, or, if not next week, certainly next month.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Somebody says "hear, hear" to support my claim. The minister was right in saying that the problem is acute,
Emergency Powers

because it has been accumulating for many years. While the Progressive Conservative party was in office from 1930 to 1935, we saw the building of houses drop from 100, if you take your base prior to the depression, down to less than 20 during those years. Our sawmills were closed; tinsmiths and carpenters joined the ranks of the unemployed because we failed to provide needed homes for Canadians at that time. We made the situation which existed during the war much more acute than it might have been, and I think it is perfectly obvious that if controls were removed the public-spirited private entrepreneurs would ship their commodities where higher prices prevail. There are other countries that are now prepared to pay higher prices for our building materials in short supply than the wartime prices and trade board regulations permit in Canada. I submit that we would have a chaotic situation in this country if the advice of the Progressive Conservative party were accepted in connection with the problem.
The former chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, Mr. Donald Gordon, in a radio address last November correctly outlined the problem that forced the government .to take action with a view to preventing [DOT]evictions for the time being, and he said that the position of landlords in Canada was not as they would have us understand. In his [DOT]speech, referring to the landlords, he said:
During the past few' years he has had very few vacancies, practically no bad debts, and has [DOT]cut down on decorating. As well, he has reduced Tenting commissions and saved some expense in unnecessary alterations and decorating which often had to be done previously to meet the whims of tenants when they were able to pick and choose.
Unfortunately our Canadian statistics do not tell us the story as far as the landlords in Canada are concerned, but in the United States the statistics over the past few years make it clear that the landlords there have had a profitable period all through the war. They have been able to pay attractive returns on their capital investments, and the fact that they had few vacancies and no trouble making their collections meant that they had a veritable gold mine. However, that set of circumstances does not curb their agitation with a view to getting rid of controls in the hope that rents might be forced to high levels and that real estate would change hands at even more highly inflated prices than now prevail.
My only comment would be to criticize the government for retreating so rapidly in this field. The federal authority should have retained firmer controls over supplies. They

turned over to the municipal authorities the problem of deciding what was an essential building and w hat was not. I remember being in Fort William and Port Arthur last fall when the most essential type of building there seemed to be poolrooms, theatres and what have you. The municipal authorities said, "What would our position be in Port Arthur, for example, if we decided1 that we could not give a permit for a theatre because it was a non-essential building? The builders would immediately go to Fort William and would have the local citizens up in arms because the city fathers had driven away a project from the city."
The federal authority was the logical one to see that, while the housing situation continued as it was, our short supplies should be diverted first of all to provide adequate housing for the people who are so crowded in all our metropolitan areas and in the towns of rural districts across the country. I think, therefore, that the comments madie by hon. members to my right fail to take into account the situation that now exists, and I am sure that the great majority of the Canadian people are behind the administration in seeing to it that rent controls are maintained and that the public are not compelled, until the housing situation has been greatly altered, to go on the streets without shelter over their heads, while those who have the largest bank accounts are placed in the position where they can get possession of the short supply of shelter.
In conclusion, the members of this group feel that they are advocating the retention of the democratic privileges of the citizen to the greatest extent by insisting that the people, through their elected representatives in, the government, should retain those controls that will be successful in keeping the cost of living down for the people of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I shall not detain the house at any great length. In fact, I had not intended taking part in the debate at this stage, were it not for the fact that this afternoon, when I attempted to ask a question of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) at the conclusion of his address, I was told to make my own speech. That is what I am doing, and I shall briefly give my opinion regarding the constitutional question about which we have heard so much this afternoon.
But before I do that, I should like to refer to some other phase of the debate which we have heard, namely the disparaging references to the so-called bureaucrats. The exposition which we had last night was, I think, a disgrace to the house. After all, the so-called bureau-

Emergency Powers
crats are our civil servants. Being a member of the banking and commerce committee, I had the privilege of getting in contact with them and to me they appeared to be decent, intelligent civil servants who were trying to do what was best for this country. Are they not responsible to a minister who is, again, responsible to this parliament? Surely these so-called bureaucrats, as well as any other civil servants, are responsible to the minister and the minister is responsible to this house. While they have been vilified by hon. members, it appears to me that no specific charge was at any time made against any of them, unless it be a charge from this particular corner of the house when we complained that some controls had been lifted which should not have been lifted; and then, if I remember aright, those actions were always taken on the responsibility of the minister himself. If we recollect the experience which we have gone through dining the war years and the two years since the war ended, it seems to me that we owe a debt of gratitude to these civil servants and these so-called bureaucrats.
As far as the constitutional question is concerned, I submit that the argument this afternoon had nothing whatever to do with the resolution before us. It seemed to be a jockeying for political advantage or position. 1 asked the hon. member for Lake Centre to read a certain part of the judgment that he had been discussing, which part is. I think, most important. When the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) on March 20 gave to this house the opinion of the deputy minister of justice, which opinion is quoted on page 1553 of Hansard, he dealt with the Agricultural Products Act and not with this particular resolution. The deputy minister of justice says in part, at the bottom of page 1553:
The true test, according to this decision-
That is, the Canada Temperance Act decision.
-is whether the real subject matter of the act goes beyond local or provincial concern and must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole. Such an act is within the competence of parliament though it may in another aspect touch upon matters specially reserved to the provinces. I should think that Bill 25 satisfies this test.
Bill No. 25 is the Agricultural Products Act. The deputy minister of justice came to this conclusion no doubt upon the following section of the decision, and I quote from the decision of the Canada Temperance Act case decided last year, as reported in Western Weekly Reports (1946) volume 2, page 6:
In their Lordships' opinion, the true test must be found in the real subject-matter of the legislation:	If it is such that it goes beyond
local or provincial concern or interests and must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole, then it will fall within the competence of the dominion parliament as a matter affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, though it may in another aspect touch upon matters specially reserved to the provincial legislatures.
As I said, the decision was quoted in the legislation concerning the Agricultuial Products Act and has nothing to do with the present resolution which is simply one based upon the emergency powers of the dominion. The decision in the Canada Temperance Act case could not by any stretch of the imagination be used as authority for the dominion parliament to legislate upon this resolution. It could not be used as authority for the dominion parliament to legislate, for instance, about rent and tenancy. Therefore I think the discussion this afternoon was altogether out of place.
While I am on my feet, may I be permitted to refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) the other night. He stated, as reported at page 1659 of Hansard:
That is why today I choose to debate the subject that socialism is contrary to human nature.
That is his opinion. I may say that I respect his opinion and I hope he will respect mine. According to the studies which I have pursued in that particular realm, there are two schools of thought or two schools of philosophy. One school says that man, the human being, is an individual and always will be. The other school says that man is a social creating. I may say that I belong to the latter school and perhaps the hon. member for Trinity belongs to the former school. The first school is particularly represented by persons such as those he quoted as authority that socialism is against human nature, and that authority is Mr. H. L. Mencken of the United States, whom I consider to be the principal proponent of this philosophy and possibly the apostle of that famous German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. I have here the book of Mencken which is a sort of biography of this philosopher Nietzsche.
The hon. member also quoted Spencer, and while I will not go so far as Mencken to interpret Spencer, this is what Mencken says at page 192:
Like Spencer before him. Nietzsche believed, as we have seen, that the best possible system of government was that which least interfered with the desires and enterprises of the efficient and intelligent individual.
Emergency Powers

Later on, at page 194 Mr. Mencken proceeds to prove some of the "freak legislation" that has been passed under democracy in some of the United States legislatures and even in congress itself. After he discusses this, he quotes the position in England and Germany, and this is what he says:
If, in England and Germany, the effect of universal suffrage has been less apparent, it is because in these countries the two upper castes have solved the problem of keeping the proletariat, despite its theoretical sovereignty, in proper leash and bounds.
If my hon. friend wishes to associate himself with this class of philosopher or with this school of philosophy, he is entitled to do so. But I believe that man is more a social creature. If you consider the annals of history from the earliest times to the present, you will see that he has made advances in his social connections and in his behaviour toward his neighbour. I fully believe that at one time or another socialism will be the ruling philosophy also in Canada.
I should like to refer here to a speech which was made almost fifteen years ago by Hon. Mr. Cahan, who was Secretary of State in the ministry of Mr. Bennett. It was during the debate on the so-called blank cheque legislation which was referred to the other day by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). In this debate the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), had implored the then Secretary of State to make his influence felt so that this legislation would not pass, because it would create a terrible precedent for some socialist government that at some time or another might hold sway in this parliament. The following day Mr. Cahan replied to that challenge, and this is what he said, as appears at page 1634 of Hansard for April 1, 1932:
But the right hon. gentleman says if we follow the precedents established in the mother of parliaments we must look forward to the time when there may be socialistic control of this parliament of Canada. I do not wish to refer to myself personally-I have passed the age of three-score years and ten and I appreciate very keenly that my mentality, my prejudices and my predilections are born of the times in which I have lived and the vicissitudes of my own personal life-but I do not look forward with any fear or shrinking to the development of socialistic institutions in this country on a proper basis. I recognize that the strain and suffering through which we have passed and are passing has already borne fruit in remedial measures, Socialistic in their tendencies, and those who are younger than I may well look forward to the time when those whose view's are more socialistic than mine will assume the reins of government in this country. When they do they will assume the reins with the voice of a great majority of the Canadian people as manifested at the polls,

they will assume office under our parliamentary institutions, not by force and violence, not by bullets and bayonets, but by the voice of the democracy of this great country. In that democracy, although I shall not live to see its development, I have the strongest possible confidence, and I think it would be a shame indeed if any minority in this house at any future time should attempt to thwart the view's of the people, should attempt to thwart necessary and essential socialistic reforms by such procedure as we have witnessed in this house during the past few W'eeks.
To be charitable, Mr. Speaker, I believe the majority of the members of the party to my right are Conservatives like Mr. Cahan, and that when the time comes they will graciously bow to the will of the majority of the Canadian people.

Probably 83166-1114
we cannot be strictly logical and consistent about the matter. Perhaps the right course to adopt is to confine the questions at this stage to broad general questions, keeping them down to as low a number as possible, and leave the more detailed questions to be asked when the bill is introduced. The procedure that is being followed here of appending fifty-seven orders in council, the number of orders in council that it was desired to continue, is, of course, unprecedented in this sense, that never has there been a situation like this to be dealt with by parliament. But I think I should point out that it is not the same kind of situation as would arise if we were attempting to introduce fifty-seven new pieces of legislation. All these orders in council are already the law of the land, and some of them have been the law of the land for seven or eight years. It would of course, be improper, if we were proposing new measures, for us to lump them together like this and cover them by one bill. But the situation is different when we are, in effect, saying that everything shall lapse but these orders in council which are already the law.
I also wish to say what I said the other night about other countries that have had the same kind of situation to deal with. Two other countries had an analogous situation, namely Great Britain and Australia, and they found, upon consideration, that this was the only way to deal with it; so they introduced bills of this type with a large number of regulations in the schedule. Provision was made for amendment of these regulations in the bills they introduced, and there were some amendments.
Perhaps the government should give a little further consideration to what might be the proper procedure to follow, so that I could state the view of the government tomorrow. Tonight I would be prepared, as far as possible, to answer questions, provided that they are of a general nature rather than concerning details. This question of the intention of the government with regard to the recovery of houses by ex-service owners is one on which I shall have to send for information from the Minister of Finance, and this illustrates the difficulties of this line of procedure. That, of course, is not something I can answer at all myself; I shall have to send for that minister, and get officials. If we were dealing with these seriatim and regularly, order by order as they are in the schedule, we would not have any such difficulty; we would start and go through them, and the minister would be here with his officials until his orders were dealt with and concluded. Anyone in the house who wanted to propose amendments
Emergency Powers

could do so; the government could either accept or reject the amendments, or they could be voted upon. Then the matter would be wound up and finished. It is pretty hard to do that here, when one hon. member gets up and asks about the eviction order; another gets up and asks about the order in council relating to old age pensions, and so on. If we are not careful we shall have no order here, and, moreover, we may have a great deal of duplication.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that the procedure you intend to follow when you bring in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When the bill is in committee we propose to take up these orders seriatim.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps a procedure something like this would work out. We might ask the Minister of Justice, who is in charge [DOT] of this resolution, general questions first and then go on to question the different ministers. The orders in council are grouped under the different ministries, and after a general questioning we might go on and question each minister about his group of orders in council. Perhaps a procedure along those lines would be satisfactory to all parties in the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wonder if I might try a suggestion, which would be that we rise and report progress, go on and deal with something else, and call a conference of the various groups to see if some arrangement could be worked out. Such a conference need not be limited to the leaders and the whips; there might be several from each party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have an hour and a half to go tonight, and we might go ahead with general questions. Then a conference can be held tomorrow in regard to further procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are you not in the position that you are trying to have a wedding without the bridegroom?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Who is the bride?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You were a fine kind of bridegroom this evening, talking against everything and voting for it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We are getting on pretty weli; leave out the cheap politics.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Lay off; you are hurting the thing, not helping.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, I am not. I just want to put forward this point of view. How can you discuss an order in council if it is not before you? These orders are not before lis. It seems to me that we have to deal with the resolution now, and I do not think you

can ask detailed questions until we have the orders in council in committee. In my judgment, just to talk about the thing in a general way is a waste of time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have the orders now.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But they are not before this committee.
