subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, no, they are not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In a kindly way may I say
we have read them all.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let the simple people have their turn. The lawyers have been at it all evening.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Labour had better get together. The Minister of Justice has admitted that the certain orders and regulations are those contained in the index and the compilation we have before us. That being so, I do not see how the Minister of Labour can get up and say that because we voted to go into committee on a resolution we voted against the principle of anything the members on this side have spoken against. How can he make his argument consistent?
While we are dealing generally with the resolution, may I ask the Minister of Justice if it is the intention of the government to leave the same men in power, with the same regulations they have administered, with the same duties to perform and the same powers, and to continue the same restrictions we have had in the past? I would submit that, if so, we shall be continuing wartime regulations, bureaucratic administration and bureaucratic legislation two years after the end of the war. So that at this stage I think the minister should be able to tell us he is going to bring about some moderation, some lessening of bureaucratic control, some restriction of the powers of various boards, not responsible to parliament, to make and interpret law which the people must obey.
Take the situation in regard to rents, for instance. Today I do not believe five per cent of Canadians, and I doubt if ten per cent of the officials administering rental control, know exactly and precisely what the law is with regard to evictions. During the last few days I personally have had great difficulty in getting anyone in Ottawa to answer certain questions, and I know there is confusion throughout this city as to what is required to raise rents, renew leases, terminate leases, evict tenants, get

Emergency Powers
possession of homes, disqualify tenants from homes on the grounds of abuse, and multifarious other matters.
My point in rising at this time is to express the opinion that, before we are through with this resolution in committee, we should know exactly and in great detail to what extent if any the Minister of Justice is prepared to lessen controls, reduce the powers of appointed officials, and remove the impediments to freedom and life and freedom of action in this country. I wonder if at this stage, in a very general way if you like, the government could not give us some indication that they realize that some of the regulations and restrictions under these fifty-seven items should be moderated or abandoned, altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know just how to answer a. question like that, containing the usual references to bureaucrats and bureaucracy, words which are terribly overworked in this house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: By the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, I say words which are terribly overworked in this house. A great many men, who are great public servants and who have rendered magnificent service to this country, are abused on the ground that they are bureaucrats. They are indiscriminately abused by certain hon. members who ought to know better, and I get very tired of hearing this indiscriminate abuse from them.
What I was going to say was this: The hon. member for Carleton asks whether I can give any indication about the future course of controls. I thought I covered that rather fully in the speech I made when I introduced the resolution. What controls will be imposed will depend upon the provisions of these orders in council which are continued. Very large numbers of orders in council are being dropped altogether, as the hon. member knows. With regard to the personnel, agents, officers and servants, in the main they will continue to be the ones who will administer these orders in council. It could not be otherwise. I do not know what is in my hon. friend's mind when he suggests anything else.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to follow the hon. member for Carleton, because I have the same point in mind. I would put a specific case to the Minister of Justice. Here we have orders in council setting up the wartime prices and trade board. I have before me the interpretation clause which, among other things, defines "offence". An offence, among other things, is a contravention of an order. And an
''order'' is set out in paragraph (k) of the section. This interpretation clause gives a long list of orders. Then we go all through the powers of the board and the obligations of citizens.
What I wish to ask is this: We are coming to the end of, or are gradually working out of, this situation. Is it necessary that all these powers, which I think we agree were necessary in war time, should be continued? Must we continue these powers? It is extremely easy for a citizen to break the law without knowing he is doing so. When I read the enforcement section of the report of the wartime prices and trade board, one of the unpleasant things I find is that, with this multitude of orders, there is an enormous number of people, ordinarily law-abiding citizens, who now find themselves, sometimes willingly I am afraid, but also sometimes perhaps unknowingly, breaking the law.
My question is this: With this huge body of orders and regulations, is there no thought of ameliorating them or softening them in any way, or are we to keep this huge body of orders and regulations to deal with what I would assume is at any rate a much smaller situation than we had before?
I might apply the same question in respect of other orders in council, but the question I have asked will indicate that I have in mind the same principle which was discussed by the hon. member for Carleton.
Mr. ILSLEk : It must be remembered that a very large number of orders are being revoked. As hon. members know, the number of orders outstanding was very great. As I said to the house, a committee of civil servants, of which the Solicitor General was chairman, was w'orking on these orders, and they have been working on them since the middle of 1945. They have succeeded in eliminating by far the greatest number of them. So that the number, which originally was several thousand-I cannot give the exact number-has been reduced to these fifty-seven.
These orders have been examined and amendments have been the result. There were many amending orders in council before they were reduced to the form in which they are now found. We think the provisions of these orders in council are substantially all necessary at- the present time. If, after examination in committee, hon. members feel that they are unnecessary, and if we are not in a position to give reasons why they are necessary, then a good case would be made for deleting them. But I do not know of such cases.
Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Did I understand (he minister to say that recently, when these orders were being consolidated to be put forward as a schedule to the bill, they were at that time scrutinized to see whether changes should even then be made ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: To accommodate them to the new situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That applies to the more important orders; I cannot speak as to the less important ones. But some of them were amended with a view to presentation to the house. That is, they were amended in such a way as to drop out sections which were no longer necessary.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It seems to me that the question before us is more one of procedure, so as to expedite the business in which we are engaged. As I watched the debate in the last few days I was comparing it with the work of the "Big Four" in Moscow. I think, really, there was a great deal more agreement among them than I have seen in this chamber. After all, I am pretty sure that if my hon. friends to my right had an opportunity to do so today, they would not abolish offhand' these orders in council.
That being so, I was going to say, "Let us be honest". I will not say that; but I will say, "Let us be reasonable, and take it for 'granted that the government was elected and is responsible for running the affairs of the country".
During my years in the house I have seen legislation go through its various stages. My experience has been that at this particular stage, when a resolution goes before the committee there is not a great deal of time taken for the consideration of it, and for the very good reason that we shall have another go at the principle of the bill when second reading is moved. Then the bill goes to the committee; and, if I am not very far wrong, hon. members to my right can take clause after clause, paragraph after paragraph, in each order in council and worry it to death, if they like. In any event, they will have ample opportunity to deal with it.
That being so, why not let this go. I was called away from the house for a short time, but I understand that in the vote this evening most of my hon. friends voted for the resolution. Why not let us be reasonable, give up this obstructionism, and let this thing go through.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it amazes me to hear the hon. member for Vancouver East talk about obstructionism, letting things go through and hurrying. If he will refer back to Hansard of March 20 he will find that the Minister of Justice and the leader of the opposition suggested that the resolution should be put into committee, right away. My leader and, I believe, the leader of the Social Credit group, were committed to that course. The leader of this part}' made that commitment, stating that we were not going to take the time of the house at that stage, but that we would let the resolution get into committee, reserving our rights to ask questions at that time, and to debate the principle of the measure on second reading. We were not committed either to approving or disapproving the principle.
Then who was it who rose in his seat and started a political dog-fight which has been going on since that time? It was the leader of the C.C.F.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a point of order, we had an important point we wanted to make, and we made it. My hon. friends did not have a point at that time, but now they have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is no point of order about that; it is merely another political speech like the ones we have been listening to here for the last several days. They started this kind of thing; they have been making political speeches right through the debate while the Speaker was in the chair and it is most amusing now to have them come along and object to anybody else taking the time of the committee. It is just typical of the procedure they carry on. They pretend to be above politics and they are the smoothest politicians in Canada; they are playing politics all the time, not only here but out in the ridings, and I think the Canadian people are beginning to realize that that is the fact.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think this-

speechtext: I am all through, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: The political part of the hon. member's speech is all finished.

speechtext:
You make your political
speeches; why object to my making one?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member, as well as all hon. members, to deal with the resolution.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There are two or three questions I should like to ask the minister. The first has to do with the time that this measure

Emergency Powers
will continue in force. As hon. members know, the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act which was passed in the fall of 1945 contained a provision to the effect that it would continue in effect until fifteen days after the commencement of the 1947 session of parliament. There was also a provision that the life of the act could be extended for a further period; but there was another unusual limitation inserted in the act which the minister will find in subsection 1 of section 6, reading as follows:
. . . for a further period, not in any case exceeding one year, from the time at which it would otherwise expire . . .
The words "not in any case exceeding" are very unusual, and I understand they were put in to make it absolutely certain that the measure would not be carried on past that time. Then in the 1946 session it was felt that the fifteen days was not a long enough time to permit legislation to be put through the house, and I think that was perfectly correct. An amendment to that section was passed extending the period to sixty days; but again we have the words, "not in any case exceeding one year," which would mean until the spring of 1948. Is that to be the limit under the new legislation? Is there to be any power taken to carry on the bill to be brought down past March 31, 1948?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There will be in the proposed bill a provision identical with the provision in the original bill and the amendment mutatis mutandis.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In English or French, does that mean that the bill may be continued until March 31, 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If addresses are presented to the Governor General by the Senate and the House of Commons respectively the bill mav be continued beyond March 31, 1948, but not for a period exceeding one year. That is the same provision as is in the present bill.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That means that the bill we are being asked to enact may be in effect until March 31, 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If parliament so orders by passing addresses.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I realize that, but I just wanted to have it clear whether it was to be until March 31, 1948, which was the time set by the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, or whether it is to be March 31, 1949. I take it from the minister's answer the year will be 1949; that will be the latest date to which this act can be carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Parliament has the right to extend it. Surely my hon. friend would not agree to deprive parliament of that right. All that the bill provides for is the continuance of the controls until 1948.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then the government may direct-

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If parliament directs by two addresses, one by this house and the other by the senate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I understood the Minister of Justice to say the other day that no new orders in council were to be passed and that these fifty-seven orders in council were not to be amended by the government, that they could only be revoked; that the cabinet would take the power under the bill to revoke any one or more of these fifty-seven orders in council.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will there be any power in the minister of reconstruction to appoint additional controllers, to decide that there should be a controller of shipping? I cite that merely as an example. speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Unless my hon. friend can
find an order in council which authorizes the government to appoint a shipping controller, it will be impossible to appoint one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I used that only as an
example.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The only controllers who
can be appointed are those for whom provision is made in the bill.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Is it the intention df the
government to appoint any additional controllers?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think the only continuing
controllers under the industries control regulations are the controller of steel and the controller of timber. If that is true those are the only controllers the government would have authority to appoint.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
P.C. 3 provides:
"Controller" means a controller heretofore appointed and now in office, or hereinafter appointed by the governor general in council.

That does not refer to any particular industry but is a general power vested in the governor in council to appoint controllers, and what I should like to know is whether it is the intention, under P.C. 3 or any other order in council, to appoint additional controllers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Let me put it in this way.
We have certain controllers now. Is power to be taken to appoint additional controllers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There are no controllers in
the wartime prices and trade board. I do not know exactly what a controller is, but I understand there are controllers under another order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Controllers are peculiar to
the Department of Munitions and Supply and are continuing their functions under the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. At the moment there is only one controller. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I agree that at the present
time there is power to appoint a steel controller and a timber controller. Is power to be taken to appoint controllers of other materials?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There is no such provision
in the order in council.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is not the intention to
take power to appoint more controllers?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would ask the Minister
of Finance whether power is to be taken to appoint additional administrators or to set up new administrative branches under the wartime prices and trade board, or are we

Emergency Powers
dealing with a structure which is not to be extended but, on the contrary, will be cut down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There are certain provisions in the bill which relate to the administration of the various orders that will be annexed, but as my colleague the Minister of Justice has said I suggest that it is perhaps not entirely appropriate to discuss the provisions of the bill until it has been given its first reading. There is, I understand, no substantial change in the provisions of the wartime prices and trade board order as it now stands, which will be one of the orders in council annexed to the bill, but I cannot say at the moment that there is no provision in the bill to provide for a new administrator of, let us say, some form of textiles or something of the kind. I am not in a position to answer that. I repeat, I think it would, be better if we dealt with that type of question when we have the bill before us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But the principle is important. It is whether the government is retaining power to appoint administrators over new materials. You have an administrator now, let us say, of textiles perhaps and wholesale goods. Is power to be taken to appoint entirely new administrators? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend can take it without fear of contradiction that it is very much on a diminishing scale. But to say that there is not power to appoint an administrator to replace an existing administrator is something I cannot say at the moment, but I can give the assurance that there is no expansion of the functions of the board contemplated but rather a marked contraction of those functions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the hon. member for Vancouver South would permit me to ask a question on the same point before he resumes, I would ask the Minister of Finance, is it not true, in spite of what he has said about the intentions of the government, that there will be in the order annexed to the bill power to extend the application of price control in case it should be necessary? I am not asking about the intentions but about the powers of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Another question has to do with the fifty-sixth and fifty-seventh orders in council. Perhaps the government would have been wise to keep it at fifty-five, because fifty-seven has unpleasant connections. But these two additional orders in council have to do with a reserve of radioactive substances. The first of them has to do with radioactive substances that may be discovered in Yukon, and the other is similar to it but applies only to the Northwest Territories. As I understand the effect of the orders in council, it is that, although the prospector may go and locate a claim and under statute law applying to Yukon get title to all the minerals in that claim, this particular order in council reserves the radioactive substances, so that he cannot get title to them. I am not quarrelling with the order in council containing that provision. It probably is a wise plan. But why should that be carried on in a temporary' measure of the type of this bill? Surely that condition is going to apply for many years. I do not understand why the government does not bring in an amendment to the Yukon Quartz Mining Act reserving radioactive substances, or an amendment to the Atomic Energy Control Act, which this house passed last year. In the latter act there are certain powers. Under section 8, paragraph (c), the board has power, with the approval of the governor in council, to acquire or cause to be acquired by purchase, lease, requisition or expropriation, prescribed substances and any mines, deposits or claims of prescribed substances; and under section 9, subsection 1, paragraph (c), the board may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations respecting mining and prospecting for prescribed substances. Obviously this provision reserving radioactive substances to the crown is of a permanent nature, and it would seem that that should be covered by an amendment to the statutes and not by continuing an order in council for a period of a year or even two years. Why is it necessary' to put these two orders in council in this bill?

There is a sharp difference of opinion on the subject. I may say that Canada is not urging that radioactive substances be controlled in the ground. Canada would prefer to rely on the provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act which provide that after radioactive material is produced it should fall within the control of the atomic energy board. The United States takes a different view and the atomic energy act of the United States-I have a memorandum on the subject-actually reserves title to uranium, thorium, et cetera in public lands. It was felt that the situation at the moment is such that Canada did not wish to legislate in a permanent way for the control of these substances in the ground. It preferred to regulate every type of control but, while the subject is rather hotly debated in the committee, it was felt that it would be wise to continue the regulation by order in council, which does control these materials in the ground, with the thought that, after a decision has been made, either the order in council can be dropped and we can rely on the present regulations of the atomic energy board, or we shall amend the regulations of the atomic energy board to provide for the control of radioactive substances in the ground.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

The minister has stated in effect that the bill which will be founded on this resolution is to limit the controls to within fifty-seven spheres. In other words, there are fifty-seven orders in council

the fifty-five in the index and two others-dealing with matters on which the government retain the right to continue controls. They do more than that; as I understand it, they retain the right to extend these controls within these various spheres, to make new controls, to
modify controls, to appoint new officers, to give new duties to new officers, to extend the duties of officers.
To illustrate my point, let me deal primarily with rental control. For some five years now' the government have adopted a system of rental control. In my opinion, they har e had ample time to figure out what controls are desired for rental control and what regulations are required to affect those controls, what officials are necessary to administer them, and what problems they are to deal with. For the past five years the public at large have allowed, or been subjected to-and I believe willingly-variations in regulations, day-to-day changes in regulations, day-to-day changes in controls, changes in the conditions under which they can get possession of their own homes, under which they can allow tenants in. can eject tenants and can extend leases. For instance, just recently the government allowed owners of commercial property to increase the rental by twenty-five per cent on certain conditions. Those conditions in some cases required the landlord or the lessor to give a five-year lease, in other cases to give a two-year lease, and in each case allowed the tenant to vacate upon thirty days' notice, but would not allow the landlord to eject the tenant under any condition.
I give that to illustrate what, to my mind, is the greatest objection the public lias to these controls; the objection is to the unknown laws of the land, the laws of the land which are being made by regulation, by administrative officers and which are not the concrete law' of the country. Consequently I believe that if the government should ask parliament today to continue the policy of rental control, they should be prepared to submit to parliament the rules and regulations under which that control is to be continued. They should allow the people of the country, the landlord and the tenant, to have some knowledge of the security of tenure the tenant has or the length of time the landlord must submit to his tenant. They must give to the public some indication, I would say, of the need of the conditions, whether it is more advantageous to the housing problem of Canada to let a tenant remain in possession of premises, or to let the landlord get possession of his own. As I see it, the returned soldier who has been fighting overseas for five years, being a young fellow may have either himself, or through his parents or friends, purchased a house, so that when he became rehabilitated he could get into a home of his own and become established. I cannot see where government policy is in any manner giving any opportunity for
Emergency Powers

the returned soldier to establish a home which he did not have when he left; and a few of them had their own homes when they left. The result is, I believe, that the government must, in order, at least, to satisfy public demand, modify that policy and let the returned soldier know at what time in the distant future he may be able to get possession of a house which he may have bought or which his father, mother or a friend may have bought for him.
I also believe that many people who are in the same category as the returned soldier brought home three or four years ago, are as much entitled to the housing accommodation as the tenants now in the premises, and that if they could occupy them it would provide just as effective an answer to the housing problem.
I give these points entirely to illustrate the fact that this government, having had five years' experience, in my humble opinion should now be prepared to set a definite policy, so that the public of Canada will know what the rules are and have some guidance as to what will be the policy for some little time in the future. You can take almost any one of the spheres of activity that these controls provide for and put up arguments similar to that. There is the wartime prices and trade board, for instance. Although we may require some controls in prices, there are many points where we do not need to leave with the officials the power to make new7 regulations, which they have. We do not need all the controls within that sphere which we have had. We should modify them to a much greater degree than this government is doing, in order to meet post war conditions. The conditions during the w7ar were vastly different.

My hon. friend has framed his question, as he said, in very general terms, and I am afraid my answer will have to be couched in somewhat similar terms. All these questions on which he has touched in connection with rental control have been under fairly intensive consideration for some time, and still are; that is to say, whether it is necessary to continue a uniform policy of control throughout the whole country, or whether it may be possible to make some relaxation in certain areas where conditions are not as acute. That whole question is being studied. So far it has not been considered desirable to modify the rental control order to provide for special regional differences. It may be possible to do so; I could not make any positive statement as to that.
On the general principle, the objective of rental control is to protect occupants of rented accommodation during this period of acute shortage. I do not think that is an overstatement, speaking of the country as a whole and perhaps particularly of the urban areas, though the condition is fairly general. I have indicated on previous occasions, as I think my colleague the Minister of Justice has indicated, that there is no intention on the part of the government to recommend the abandonment of either rental control or eviction control as long as such conditions continue to exist. But it is a brave man who will constitute himself a prophet as to exactly when conditions will be such that these controls can be either lifted entirely, or the point at which they can be relaxed from time to time. But I repeat the assurance I have given before in connection with other controls, that they will be relaxed just as soon as we believe we can do so in justice to the people of Canada, for whom we have some responsibility. Certainly no one will be more pleased than myself and some of the people who have had to administer these rental controls when it is found possible to take this action.
I am sorry I cannot be more specific in answer to my hon. friend's question, but I doubt whether he really expected me to be.

We plain, simple folk read
a thing and understand it as it was intended. I should like to ask the minister one simple question about the resolution, just so that he will not forget there is a resolution before the committee. He is likely to begin discussing the bill and I want to bring the minister back to the resolution. Certain orders are going to be carried forward for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war. Who is to define or decide when that national emergency has ceased to exist? I am thinking back to September 10, 1939, when a much greater national emergency existed than exists today. Am I to assume that the national emergency will not be over until we get back to the economic stagnation that existed prior to 1939? Am I wrong in assuming that that is where my hon. friends to my right want to go? I wish to be sure that that is not what the minister has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is not what the government has in mind.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On page 11 of this bill-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We are not discussing the bill.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We are discussing what is to come before the house in a short time and it seems to me that we should be able lo find
Emergency Powers

out what we are to be dealing with. For instance, we are to be dealing with returned soldiers who receive appointments under the civil service. In the omnibus bill that is before us there are five or six different orders in council, some of which go back to 1927. We are now in the year 1947. When we come to the omnibus bill are we to deal with this matter in this hit-or-miss way that we are dealing with at the present time, or are we to have these bundled together and put before us in the form of a statute so that those who run may read? If the minister would answer that, then I should like to ask one other question.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The Civil Service Act will be amended eventually, but we do not want to take a chance of veterans preference lapsing. Consequently the orders in council which have existed during the war will be continued under the omnibus bill so that there will be no chance of that preference lapsing between the time the orders run out and the time the amendment to the Civil Service Act is brought before the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Will this act be consolidated some time during the discussion? Shall we have something before us to crystallize it in one form? After all, it is not fair that one should have to go through five or six different orders in council to find out the position of the returned soldier.
Mr. ILbLEY: When the bill is introduced I will lay on the table copies of the orders in council and the amending orders in council. For the convenience of hon. members, the orders in council as amended have been consolidated in office consolidations which have been circulated. Each hon. member has before him this office consolidation which is a most convenient, source of information to consult. There will also be on the table of the house the orders in council and the amending orders in council as they appear in the schedule to the bill. Even-thing has been done to place before the members of the house exactly what they will be dealing with.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am sorry to have to refer to this omnibus bill but I am not going to speak about it. There are wartime leasehold l emulations dealing with both commercial and residential properties. There are two orders which set out the regulations. Shall we have before us those regulations which at the present time are dealt with by orders in council dealing with housing and commercial accommodation? Shall we have those orders before us so that we may know where we are going and what we are discussing? We should know whether the department has decided to
fMr. Timmins.]
make any changes. The Minister of Finance, if I understood his words correctly, said that the department is discussing whether or not changes will be made before the bill is put before us. Are we to have all the orders dealing with those two fields before us?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: All the board orders should be produced by the minister. This house is entitled to them if they want them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will they not be produced so that we may know about them at the beginning?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know what the house wants yet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think we want everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is a library here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I agree fully with what the Minister of Justice said. We do not want to go over the course twice, but I submit that there are a few things which, if we could clear in our minds about them now, would perhaps save time later. There are one or two which I think are worth mentioning now. One thing that will be important when we come to the wartime prices and trade board orders in council is the cost figures which appear in the report of that board. I presume I should address my remarks to the Minister of Finance, so I shall ask him if he would have the figures on page 55 which show the rises in prices reconsidered. From a remark made by Mr. Gordon the other day in the banking and commerce committee, I understand that these figures do not contain anything to indicate the subsidies which have been paid. In other words, if the subsidies paid were included in these figures they would show a different figure.
I do not know whether anyone else has had this experience, but I know I have had it and some of my friends have had it. When she is told that the cost of food had risen from August, 1945, to the end of 1946 by only 6-8 per cent, my wife, whom I have always considered to be a sensible woman, just smiles.
I am not suggesting that there are any wrong figures there and I am not criticizing the bureaucrats or officials, but I am suggesting that it is possible to include figures which are not really typical ones. I have had inquiry made and I confess I am puzzled about the figures showing the rise in the cost of food in Canada from the pre-war figures to the end of 1946. This is given as forty-five per cent. I have had a figure made by a person who, I think, is a reliable person. I admit it is hard to be sure that you have all the

Emergency Powers
figures, but at any rate the result arrived at is a much larger figure. I suggest that when we come to consider this matter these figures will be important because they are relevant to the consideration of the full picture.
I suggest to the minister that he might have these figures looked up, and in particular I suggest that care be taken to include the subsidy figures. To my mind, these figures are realiy misleading if the subsidy figures are not taken in. Otherwise we have not a fair comparison with the United States, and if we could get that it would be useful to us when we come to discuss the bill itself.
There is one other question I would raise in regard to the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation. The order in council with regard to that is long, and wide powers are given. Then 1 look at the schedule and at the report of the wartime prices and trade board. I am not quite sure that I have it all clear but, as far as I can make out, a large number of items are said to be ineligible for subsidies; in other words, the subsidies are no longer to be continued. I raise the question whether these extraordinary powers are needed to do what is now a much smaller task. In answer to my question some time ago the Minister of Justice said that thought had been given to seeing whether all the powers previously conveyed during the war were necessary to continue with the much smaller task now.
I turn to page 20 of the consolidation of the orders in council to draw attention to the extraordinary variety of things which are included1 as "services" such as laundering, cleaning, tailoring and dressmaking; hairdressing and beauty parlour services; the pasteurizing of honey on a custom or commission basis. I am not going to take time to read more, but I am asking seriously whether these astonishing powers which lead to lawbreaking on a large scale, as referred to in the report of the prices board, are necessary. I know we are continuing them for only one year, but I am asking whether all these powers are necessary or not.
I am going to make a suggestion on detail. I think it would be useful to us, when we come to what will be the arduous task of considering the bill, if it would not be possible in some way, purely as a matter of mechanical convenience, to show not merely the original orders, not merely the consolidation which the minister says we shall have in addition to the detailed orders, but also what deletions have been made and what powers have been restricted. If there is some way in which that can be shown it would greatly simplify our task.
I should like to add one word. The minister said that these orders had been scrutinized to see if certain deletions could be made. The powers are still so ample, so detailed, so meticulous, that it is hard for me to believe that they are all now required. Certain restrictions and deletions may have been made. If so, I suggest that they be shown in some way so that they can be easily picked out and we shall understand what has happened.
I should like in particular for the Minister of Finance to comment on these figures to which I referred on page 55 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board and make whatever comment on them he wishes. I shall be glad if he would say whether he would have those further figures prepared, for which I have asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend intends me to comment on them tonight. He has called my attention to these figures and indicated his desire that at the appropriate stage, I take it. I should be prepared to comment on them. I shall be glad to do that. Probably the better time would be on the second reading of the bill or. better still, in committee on the bill, when I can have the controller here to elaborate and enlarge on any figures on which my hon. friend may want special information.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was not expecting the minister to answer out of his head now, but I am suggesting that it is a reasonable request and might be convenient if these figures could be prepared and be read}- for us when we are considering the bill, which I presume will be a matter of days yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, just as soon as we get through with this discussion we shall introduce the bill. It will have to stand a day before the second reading is taken.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You will go right ahead with the second reading?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, unless there is a request for more time, which, of course, we would be willing to give.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then my suggestion is this. We ought to be given these figures as soon as possible. I think they are relevant and they might be important. They are not easy for us to come by. There are different views as to how they should be made up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not quite clear as to what figures my hon. friend wants, but I had
Emergency Powers

n mind reading his remarks in Hansard and considering them. If they are figures which are not in the report but are available they will, of course, be provided.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I will read the figures I have in mind. They are at page 55 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board. First of all, they are the figures in Canada and in the United States from August, 1945, to December, 1946. I will read two typical figures: general wholesale prices, showing a rise in Canada of 7-5 and in the United States of 32-1. Then you come to retail food, showing a rise in Canada of 6-8 and in the United States of 31-9. That retail food figure will be substantially raised if the food subsidies are taken into it, as I understood Mr. Gordon to say the other day. I find it difficult to understand these figures because they are quite different from figures that I have had prepared by competent persons who worked hard and who arrived, quite apart from the subsidies, at quite a different figure. I should like to know how these figures are made up. I think it is important that we should have them because we do not want to be asking about figures when we are in the midst of discussing the orders in council.
Progress reported.
